screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn why event listening is a core technique for reactive Fabric client applications. Instead of polling the ledger, listeners deliver near real-time notifications when something important happens, like asset creation or transaction commits. By the end you'll know which listener to choose, how to implement it, and how to keep your application resilient. Consider an app that should only react to business events — which listener will you pick, and why?

screens.title: Why Event Listening Replaces Polling
screens.narratorSegment: Event listening is a strategy where client applications subscribe to notifications emitted by the Fabric network instead of repeatedly polling the ledger for changes. This matters because polling creates continuous load on peers and introduces delay between the ledger change and the client response. For example, a supply-chain dashboard that polls every ten seconds may still show stale data between polls, and it will generate many redundant queries. An event listener, by contrast, receives a push notification the moment the peer commits a block or a chaincode emits a business event, enabling immediate UI refresh or downstream processing. A useful mental model: polling is a scanner checking the ledger periodically, while listening is a subscription that receives an alert only on relevant activity. One misconception is to treat listeners as guaranteed instant delivery; network interruptions or peer differences can delay or drop events, so your application should include fallback strategies and verify state when necessary. In practice, combine chaincode listeners for targeted business events with occasional reconciliation queries when strict finality or completeness is required. As a reflective question: if your application requires a complete audit trail of all transactions, which listener type and additional step would you use?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Why Event Listening
Definition

Event listening lets clients subscribe to notifications from Fabric peers for blocks or chaincode events, enabling reactive updates without repeated ledger queries.

Analogy
Think of polling as checking a ticket office for updates every minute. Listening is signing up for a text alert that a ticket is available — fewer checks and faster reaction.
When to listen
UIs, webhooks, and integrations that must react quickly to ledger changes.
When to poll
Periodic reconciliation tasks, or when connectivity is intermittent and a full scan is acceptable.
Concrete Example
A dashboard that must update immediately after CreateAsset should subscribe to the AssetCreated chaincode event. Use chaincode listeners to receive the event payload and refresh the UI exactly when the transaction commits.
Common misconception
Listeners guarantee order and delivery. In reality, delivery timing may vary between peers; use block numbers or reconcile state for strict ordering.
Key Takeaway

Prefer listeners for timely updates, but include reconciliation when completeness and strict ordering matter.

screens.title: Block Listeners
screens.narratorSegment: A block listener subscribes to notifications whenever a new block is committed to the ledger on a specific channel. A Block object contains the block header with its number and an array of transaction envelopes. Listening to blocks gives your application a complete view of activity on the channel, which is useful for auditing, analytics, or systems that must react to all transactions regardless of the specific chaincode invoked. When you process a block you typically inspect the block. header. number for ordering, iterate over block. data. data to see transactions, and examine each transaction's payload header to find transaction IDs and chaincode identifiers. One trade-off is verbosity: block listeners can produce a lot of data, so they are less efficient when you only need specific business events. A common mistake is to assume chaincode name is always present in the channel header; parsing logic should be defensive. Example: a logging service adds a block listener, logs Tx ID and type for each transaction, and uses block number to preserve order. Key takeaway: use block listeners for full visibility, and use careful parsing to avoid runtime errors when transaction structures vary.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Block Listeners
What a Block contains
  • header.number — the block sequence number used for ordering.
  • data.data — array of transaction envelopes within the block.
  • validation codes — status of each transaction commit for auditing.
When to use
Audit logs, analytics pipelines, and any system that must process every transaction on a channel.
Example parsing flow
Iterate over block.data.data, for each transaction unwrap payload.data and header.channel_header to extract tx_id and typeString. Log block header number to preserve ordering across messages.
Example code sketch
// network.addBlockListener('id', (block) => {
//   console.log(`Block ${block.header.number}`)
//   block.data.data.forEach(txEnvelope => { /* inspect payload.header.channel_header */ })
// })
Common Mistake

Treating block listeners as lightweight. They can generate large volumes of events; filter or route only what you need.

screens.title: Block Listener Code Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical Node. js pattern for adding a block listener and parsing its contents. After obtaining a Network object from the Gateway, call network. addBlockListener with a listener name and a callback that receives the Block object. Inside the callback you typically log the block. header. number so you can rely on it for ordering. Then iterate over block. data. data, which contains the transaction envelopes. For each envelope, reach into payload. data and then payload. header. channel_header to find tx_id, typeString, and optionally chaincode identifiers. Wrap parsing in defensive checks because some blocks or envelopes may not have the fields you expect. For long-running applications remember to keep a reference to the returned listener and call network. removeBlockListener(listener) when the app no longer needs notifications. A concrete snippet from the chapter logs the block number and the Tx ID for each transaction; it also demonstrates storing the listener in a variable so you can remove it in finally. Misconception: adding many unnamed listeners without removing them can exhaust connections. Always name and manage listener instances. Try the code by submitting a transaction and watching the console print the block and transaction details.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Block Listener Walkthrough
Full example (excerpt)
// Add a block listener
const blockListener = await network.addBlockListener('my-block-listener', (block) => {
  console.log(`Block ${block.header.number} received. Contains ${block.data.data.length} transactions.`)
  block.data.data.forEach(transactionEnvelope => {
    const payload = transactionEnvelope.payload.data
    const channelHeader = payload.header.channel_header
    console.log(`Tx ID: ${channelHeader.tx_id}, Type: ${channelHeader.typeString}`)
  })
})
// Later: await network.removeBlockListener(blockListener)
Parsing checklist
  • Check block.header.number exists before using it for ordering.
  • Verify block.data and block.data.data are arrays before iterating.
  • Guard access to payload.header.channel_header to avoid undefined errors.
Pro Tip
Log a concise summary per block (number, tx count) rather than each field to keep logs readable, then inspect individual transactions when needed.
Key Takeaway

Block listeners reveal every transaction in order. Parse defensively and remove listeners when not in use.

screens.title: Chaincode Events and SetEvent
screens.narratorSegment: Chaincode events are custom notifications emitted by chaincode during transaction execution using a SetEvent call on the transaction stub. These events are application-defined and typically carry a name plus a payload that encodes domain information, for example asset metadata. Emitting an event from the CreateAsset function using SetEvent with a payload such as the newly-created asset's JSON allows clients to subscribe only to meaningful business changes. The chapter shows a Go chaincode snippet that calls ctx. GetStub(). SetEvent("AssetCreated", assetJSON). The important points are: choose event names that reflect business actions; keep payloads concise and structured (JSON is common); and know that the SDK receives the payload as a Buffer, so clients must convert it to string before parsing. A common misconception is to emit events for every minor state update; prefer events for changes consumers actually care about to avoid noise. Example: emit AssetCreated only when a new asset enters the ledger and not for internal transient steps. The final takeaway: chaincode events give you precise, business-level hooks that map directly to application workflows. Chaincode Events and SetEvent means use setevent in chaincode to emit named events with payloads that clients can subscribe to for targeted reactions.. In practical terms, emit business events from chaincode with setevent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Chaincode Events
Go chaincode example
func (s *SmartContract) CreateAsset(ctx contractapi.TransactionContextInterface, id string, color string, size int, owner string, appraisedValue int) error {
    // ... asset creation logic ...
    err = ctx.GetStub().SetEvent("AssetCreated", assetJSON)
    if err != nil {
        return fmt.Errorf("failed to set event: %v", err)
    }
    return nil
}
Best practices
  • Use clear, business-oriented event names such as AssetCreated or AssetTransferred.
  • Keep payloads compact and JSON-serializable for easier parsing by clients.
  • Emit events only for changes that downstream consumers need.
Common Mistake

Emitting too many low-value events creates noise. Keep events meaningful to consumers to reduce processing overhead.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Chaincode Listener Walkthrough
Client example (excerpt)
// Add a chaincode event listener
const chaincodeListener = await contract.addContractListener('my-chaincode-listener', (event) => {
  console.log(`Event Name: ${event.eventName}`)
  console.log(`Transaction ID: ${event.transactionId}`)
  if (event.payload) {
    console.log(`Payload: ${event.payload.toString()}`)
    try {
      const parsed = JSON.parse(event.payload.toString())
      console.log(`Parsed Asset ID: ${parsed.ID}`)
    } catch (jsonError) {
      console.error(`Failed to parse event payload: ${jsonError.message}`)
    }
  }
}, { filtered: false })
Key notes
  • Use filtered: false to receive the full payload Buffer; convert it before parsing.
  • Wrap JSON.parse in try-catch to avoid listener crashes from malformed payloads.
  • Keep the listener instance to remove it with contract.removeContractListener when done.
Common Mistake

Assuming payload is a string. The SDK gives a Buffer; always call toString() before parsing.

screens.title: filtered Option and Payload Choices
screens.narratorSegment: The addContractListener call accepts an options object with a filtered flag that controls whether the listener receives the full event payload or minimal metadata. If filtered is true, the listener receives only the event name and transaction ID; this reduces bandwidth and may be sufficient when the client only needs to know that an event occurred. If filtered is false, the SDK delivers the full payload Buffer exactly as chaincode set it, which is usually necessary when you need event details such as asset fields. The chapter recommends filtered false for most applications because you typically want the payload content — but be mindful of payload size and security. Always treat the payload as untrusted input: convert it from Buffer using toString(), then wrap JSON. parse in try-catch to handle malformed data. A common misconception is that filtered true means higher security — it only limits delivered data, it does not validate payload integrity. Choose filtered based on data needs and network constraints. Example: a mobile client with limited bandwidth might use filtered true and then fetch details only for interesting events.

keyIdea.text: Use filtered:false when you need event payloads; use filtered:true to reduce data for minimal notifications, but plan a follow-up fetch if details are needed.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › filtered Option
filtered: true
Delivers only minimal info such as event name and transaction ID. Good for low-bandwidth clients or when only the occurrence matters.
When to use
Mobile notifications, simple counters, or when you will fetch details on demand.
filtered: false
Delivers the full payload Buffer as set by SetEvent. Use when clients need the event data immediately, such as dashboards or downstream processing.
When to use
Dashboards, integration services, and workflows that react to payload contents.
Pro Tip

If using filtered:true, plan a safe follow-up query to fetch details for important events. If using filtered:false, validate and limit payload size to avoid overloading clients.

screens.title: Managing Listener Lifecycle
screens.narratorSegment: Listener lifecycle management prevents resource leaks and unexpected behavior. When you add listeners with network. addBlockListener or contract. addContractListener, keep the returned listener instance in a variable so you can remove it later. For short-lived scripts or when a user logs out, call network. removeBlockListener(listener) and contract. removeContractListener(listener) in a finally block during cleanup to close open connections. content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.7 › Listener Lifecycle
Lifecycle checklist
  1. Declare variables for listener instances before registering.
  2. Register listeners and keep returned instances for later removal.
  3. Call removeBlockListener / removeContractListener in finally or shutdown hooks.
  4. Disconnect the gateway after cleanup to close connections.
Example pattern
let blockListener
let chaincodeListener
try {
  blockListener = await network.addBlockListener('my-block-listener', callback)
  chaincodeListener = await contract.addContractListener('my-chaincode-listener', callback, { filtered:false })
  // submit transactions...
} finally {
  if (blockListener) await network.removeBlockListener(blockListener)
  if (chaincodeListener) await contract.removeContractListener(chaincodeListener)
  if (gateway) await gateway.disconnect()
}
Key Takeaway

Always remove listeners in cleanup paths. This prevents resource leaks and avoids leaving open streams to peers.

screens.title: Error Handling and Connection Stability
screens.narratorSegment: Error handling inside listener callbacks is critical because unhandled exceptions can crash the listener or the application. When processing a block or chaincode event, wrap your parsing and business logic in try-catch blocks and log meaningful diagnostics so you can investigate malformed data or unexpected payload shapes. For JSON payloads always perform event. payload. toString() and then JSON. parse in try-catch. For network stability, listeners rely on an open connection to the peer. If the peer or network drops, your listener may stop receiving events. Implement reconnection strategies that attempt to re-register listeners after transient failures, and ensure your application can tolerate temporary gaps by reconciling state, for example by checking ledger state after re-establishing a listener. A common misconception is that listeners are automatically persistent across restarts or peer failover. In practice, you must re-register listeners after reconnecting. For production systems, monitor listener health and include exponential backoff for reconnection attempts. The final practical point: always include cleanup and reconnection logic to keep your eventing robust in real environments. screens.title: Event Ordering and Guarantees
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding ordering is essential when multiple peers or listeners are involved. Events emitted from within a single block preserve an order, but the timing of when different peers deliver events to clients can vary. For strict ordering requirements rely on block. header. number and, where needed, the transaction index within the block rather than on wall-clock delivery times. For example, if you need to apply transactions in the exact ledger order in a downstream system, attach block number and transaction metadata from the block listener and use that ordering to process events deterministically. A misconception is to assume the order of arrival equals ledger order; it does not. Also, chaincode events are tied to transactions and will appear in the block containing that transaction. If you need cross-peer consistency, reconcile using ledger queries keyed by block number and transaction ID after receiving notifications. In short: use ledger metadata for ordering guarantees and treat delivery timing as an unreliable transport attribute that needs confirmation against the ledger when correctness matters. Event Ordering and Guarantees means use block numbers and transaction indices to determine true ledger order. do not rely on delivery timing between peers for strict ordering guarantees.. screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these three core ideas top of mind. First, event listening is the recommended way to get real-time updates from Fabric: it reduces polling overhead and enables responsive applications. Second, block listeners deliver every transaction committed on a channel and are ideal for auditing and analytics, while chaincode listeners capture business-level events emitted by SetEvent and are the efficient choice for dashboards and workflows. Third, manage listeners carefully: convert payload Buffers to strings, parse JSON inside try-catch, use the filtered option wisely, and always remove listeners and disconnect the gateway to avoid resource leaks. These practices together let you build reliable, efficient, and maintainable Fabric client applications that respond to ledger changes quickly and safely. As a practical habit, when you add a listener, write the cleanup code immediately so you never forget to remove it.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn why event listening is a core technique for reactive Fabric client applications. Instead of polling the ledger, listeners deliver near real-time notifications when something important happens, like asset creation or transaction commits. That reduces latency and avoids repeated expensive queries. You will see two complementary listener types: block listeners that surface every committed block and chaincode listeners that surface business events emitted by chaincode using SetEvent. We will show how to add listeners with the Node. js SDK, how to parse Buffer payloads safely, and how to manage listener lifecycle to avoid resource leaks. A concrete example is a dashboard that must refresh immediately after a CreateAsset transaction emits an AssetCreated event; a chaincode listener filters for that event and updates UI state directly, while a block listener can power audit logs or analytics where every transaction matters. I will also highlight common pitfalls: forgetting to remove listeners, not converting payloads from Buffer, and relying on peer timing for ordering. By the end you'll know which listener to choose, how to implement it, and how to keep your application resilient. Consider an app that should only react to business events — which listener will you pick, and why?

These objectives guide the hands-on and conceptual work you will do. First, you will explain why event listening is important for real-time updates and asynchronous processing, and when it beats polling. Second, you will distinguish between block events and chaincode events, and describe the use cases that call for each. Third, you will implement event listeners with the Node. js SDK: adding a block listener on a Network object and adding a contract listener for chaincode events. Fourth, you will parse event payloads safely from Buffer to string and, when appropriate, JSON, while managing listener lifecycle and errors. Each objective includes a short practical task: identify whether a dashboard needs a chaincode listener, add a block listener to log transactions, implement payload parsing with try-catch, and remove listeners on logout or process exit. Together these skills let you build Fabric clients that react reliably to ledger changes, minimize wasted resources, and surface only the events your application needs.

This page lists concrete practice milestones that map directly to the chapter's learning objectives. For each skill you will complete a short task: first, explain the trade-off between polling and event listening in a short paragraph and give an example where polling still makes sense. Second, create a checklist that compares when to use a block listener versus a chaincode listener for monitoring, auditing, and dashboard updates. Third, open the sample app. js and add a network. addBlockListener and contract. addContractListener, then submit transactions to observe output. Fourth, implement payload parsing that converts Buffer to string and wraps JSON. parse in try-catch, and remove listeners at the end of the script to avoid leaks. These tasks are intentionally small so you can complete one per coding session and confirm behavior locally. Each milestone is a verified competency: you should be able to run node app. js, observe the correct console messages, and explain why each listener triggered. This practice connects conceptual understanding with real-world diagnostics and reduces the chance of mistakes in production deployments.

Event listening is a strategy where client applications subscribe to notifications emitted by the Fabric network instead of repeatedly polling the ledger for changes. This matters because polling creates continuous load on peers and introduces delay between the ledger change and the client response. For example, a supply-chain dashboard that polls every ten seconds may still show stale data between polls, and it will generate many redundant queries. An event listener, by contrast, receives a push notification the moment the peer commits a block or a chaincode emits a business event, enabling immediate UI refresh or downstream processing. A useful mental model: polling is a scanner checking the ledger periodically, while listening is a subscription that receives an alert only on relevant activity. One misconception is to treat listeners as guaranteed instant delivery; network interruptions or peer differences can delay or drop events, so your application should include fallback strategies and verify state when necessary. In practice, combine chaincode listeners for targeted business events with occasional reconciliation queries when strict finality or completeness is required. As a reflective question: if your application requires a complete audit trail of all transactions, which listener type and additional step would you use?

A block listener subscribes to notifications whenever a new block is committed to the ledger on a specific channel. A Block object contains the block header with its number and an array of transaction envelopes. Listening to blocks gives your application a complete view of activity on the channel, which is useful for auditing, analytics, or systems that must react to all transactions regardless of the specific chaincode invoked. When you process a block you typically inspect the block. header. number for ordering, iterate over block. data. data to see transactions, and examine each transaction's payload header to find transaction IDs and chaincode identifiers. One trade-off is verbosity: block listeners can produce a lot of data, so they are less efficient when you only need specific business events. A common mistake is to assume chaincode name is always present in the channel header; parsing logic should be defensive. Example: a logging service adds a block listener, logs Tx ID and type for each transaction, and uses block number to preserve order. Key takeaway: use block listeners for full visibility, and use careful parsing to avoid runtime errors when transaction structures vary.

Let's walk through a practical Node. js pattern for adding a block listener and parsing its contents. After obtaining a Network object from the Gateway, call network. addBlockListener with a listener name and a callback that receives the Block object. Inside the callback you typically log the block. header. number so you can rely on it for ordering. Then iterate over block. data. data, which contains the transaction envelopes. For each envelope, reach into payload. data and then payload. header. channel_header to find tx_id, typeString, and optionally chaincode identifiers. Wrap parsing in defensive checks because some blocks or envelopes may not have the fields you expect. For long-running applications remember to keep a reference to the returned listener and call network. removeBlockListener(listener) when the app no longer needs notifications. A concrete snippet from the chapter logs the block number and the Tx ID for each transaction; it also demonstrates storing the listener in a variable so you can remove it in finally. Misconception: adding many unnamed listeners without removing them can exhaust connections. Always name and manage listener instances. Try the code by submitting a transaction and watching the console print the block and transaction details.

Chaincode events are custom notifications emitted by chaincode during transaction execution using a SetEvent call on the transaction stub. These events are application-defined and typically carry a name plus a payload that encodes domain information, for example asset metadata. Emitting an event from the CreateAsset function using SetEvent with a payload such as the newly-created asset's JSON allows clients to subscribe only to meaningful business changes. The chapter shows a Go chaincode snippet that calls ctx. GetStub(). SetEvent("AssetCreated", assetJSON). The important points are: choose event names that reflect business actions; keep payloads concise and structured (JSON is common); and know that the SDK receives the payload as a Buffer, so clients must convert it to string before parsing. A common misconception is to emit events for every minor state update; prefer events for changes consumers actually care about to avoid noise. Example: emit AssetCreated only when a new asset enters the ledger and not for internal transient steps. The final takeaway: chaincode events give you precise, business-level hooks that map directly to application workflows. Chaincode Events and SetEvent means use setevent in chaincode to emit named events with payloads that clients can subscribe to for targeted reactions.. In practical terms, emit business events from chaincode with setevent. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

On the client side, the Node. js SDK exposes contract. addContractListener to receive chaincode events. You typically register the listener after obtaining a Contract object. When the listener callback runs it receives an event object that contains eventName, transactionId, and a payload Buffer when filtered is false. Convert the payload with event. payload. toString(), then parse JSON inside a try-catch if you expect structured data. The example from the chapter registers a listener named my-chaincode-listener and logs event. eventName and event. transactionId. It demonstrates handling parsing errors and printing parsed fields like the asset ID. Remember the filtered option: when filtered is true you receive only minimal information; filtered false returns the full payload and is the usual choice when you need payload content. Also save the returned listener instance and remove it with contract. removeContractListener(listener) when finished. A common misconception is that filtered false always includes every field; it returns the payload as set by SetEvent but network configuration can affect availability. Practice by emitting AssetCreated from chaincode and watching the client print the parsed asset details. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The addContractListener call accepts an options object with a filtered flag that controls whether the listener receives the full event payload or minimal metadata. If filtered is true, the listener receives only the event name and transaction ID; this reduces bandwidth and may be sufficient when the client only needs to know that an event occurred. If filtered is false, the SDK delivers the full payload Buffer exactly as chaincode set it, which is usually necessary when you need event details such as asset fields. The chapter recommends filtered false for most applications because you typically want the payload content — but be mindful of payload size and security. Always treat the payload as untrusted input: convert it from Buffer using toString(), then wrap JSON. parse in try-catch to handle malformed data. A common misconception is that filtered true means higher security — it only limits delivered data, it does not validate payload integrity. Choose filtered based on data needs and network constraints. Example: a mobile client with limited bandwidth might use filtered true and then fetch details only for interesting events.

Understanding ordering is essential when multiple peers or listeners are involved. Events emitted from within a single block preserve an order, but the timing of when different peers deliver events to clients can vary. For strict ordering requirements rely on block. header. number and, where needed, the transaction index within the block rather than on wall-clock delivery times. For example, if you need to apply transactions in the exact ledger order in a downstream system, attach block number and transaction metadata from the block listener and use that ordering to process events deterministically. A misconception is to assume the order of arrival equals ledger order; it does not. Also, chaincode events are tied to transactions and will appear in the block containing that transaction. If you need cross-peer consistency, reconcile using ledger queries keyed by block number and transaction ID after receiving notifications. In short: use ledger metadata for ordering guarantees and treat delivery timing as an unreliable transport attribute that needs confirmation against the ledger when correctness matters. Keep these three core ideas top of mind. First, event listening is the recommended way to get real-time updates from Fabric: it reduces polling overhead and enables responsive applications. Second, block listeners deliver every transaction committed on a channel and are ideal for auditing and analytics, while chaincode listeners capture business-level events emitted by SetEvent and are the efficient choice for dashboards and workflows. Third, manage listeners carefully: convert payload Buffers to strings, parse JSON inside try-catch, use the filtered option wisely, and always remove listeners and disconnect the gateway to avoid resource leaks. These practices together let you build reliable, efficient, and maintainable Fabric client applications that respond to ledger changes quickly and safely.
